title: Iraq Declares Sept 30 US Withdrawal 'Final', Hormuz Transit Collapses to Eight Ships, North Korea Fires Missile
subhead: Baghdad locks in the end of the US-led coalition's military mission, Hormuz traffic hits a one-week low as Iran holds firm, and Pyongyang tests again ahead of US-South Korea drills.

sections.heading: Iraq Sets a Hard Date for the End of the US Military Presence
sections.body:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the September 30 deadline for ending the US-led coalition's military mission in Iraq and completing the withdrawal of its forces is 'fixed and final', according to a statement from his office after a meeting with US Central Command chief General Brad Cooper. A US official confirmed to the Associated Press that Washington expects to complete its pullout by September 30, though it declined to say how many troops remain or where they would be redeployed.

The statement framed October 1 as 'a new day in the trajectory of the Iraqi state, as Iraq will be free of any foreign military presence', and called placing all weapons under exclusive state control 'an essential prerequisite' for the next phase. The withdrawal would close a US presence that began with the 2003 invasion and was rebuilt after ISIL's 2014 rise; US forces already left most Iraqi bases last year but kept a footprint in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region, where bases have come under repeated attack since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February.
sections.whyItMatters: A firm, publicly confirmed end date for the US military mission in Iraq removes a major pillar of Washington's regional posture at the height of the Iran war, and shifts the burden of containing armed groups onto Baghdad's state security forces.

sections.heading: Hormuz Transit Hits a One-Week Low as Trump and Iran Trade Control Claims
sections.body:
Just eight ships transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, far below the 130 to 140 vessels that crossed daily before the war, according to Reuters, citing trade analytics platform Kpler. President Donald Trump insisted in a Truth Social post that the US has 'total control' over the strait and called the blockade of Iranian ports 'A WALL OF STEEL', while Iran's new security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said the strait will not reopen until the US ends the war and blockade, releases frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire including Lebanon and Gaza.

Iran continues to pursue separate talks with Oman on the strait's future management, which Tehran insists are distinct from any deal with Washington. Pakistan's foreign ministry said it is working to 'bring the two parties to the negotiating table', with its interior minister visiting Tehran. Analysts, including Dennis Citrinowicz of the Institute for National Security Studies, warned that the drive to frame the conflict as a victory is creating a 'virtual reality' that prevents decisions based on the situation on the ground.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Washington's rhetoric and the reality of near-empty shipping lanes is widening, and with talks stalled and Iran holding firm on its conditions, the economic cost of the closure continues to mount.

sections.heading: Houthis Kill Six in First Deadly Shipping Attack of the War
sections.body:
Yemen's internationally recognised government accused the Houthis of killing at least six people and wounding ten in a double-tap strike on the Egyptian-owned cargo vessel Tihamah in the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Yemen's Transport Ministry said three Pakistani nationals and one Indonesian national were killed after three ballistic missiles hit the ship, and the coastguard said a second missile struck the rescue operation, killing at least two troops responding to the first attack.

The deaths are the first shipping fatalities linked to the Houthis since the US-Israel war on Iran began on February 28. Yemen's Foreign Ministry called on the international community to move 'from condemnation to effective and decisive action'. The attack follows the collapse of the UN-backed 2022 truce in Yemen's civil war, which unravelled after a Saudi air strike on Sanaa airport on July 13.
sections.whyItMatters: The first confirmed deaths from Houthi maritime attacks mark a qualitative escalation in the Red Sea front, raising the stakes for shipping insurers and for any effort to restore safe passage.

sections.heading: Ukraine Pounds Novorossiysk Grain Terminals and Sends New Peace Proposals to Washington
sections.body:
Ukraine launched a massive overnight drone and missile attack on Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, killing three people including a child and wounding at least 24, according to regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev. Ukraine's SBU security service called the strike of 'strategic significance', and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other vessels were hit. Russia's defence ministry said it downed 502 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Separately, Zelenskyy said Kyiv has handed the United States new proposals to end the four-and-a-half-year war, focused on strengthening Ukraine's air defences and increasing pressure on Moscow. He also accused Russia of planning to use its parliamentary elections next month as a pretext for a new mobilisation of 'several hundred thousand' troops by year's end. In a related development, President Trump announced that Russia released former US Marine Robert Gilman after four years in detention, with Washington releasing no prisoners in return.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's strikes on Russia's grain export hub threaten global wheat supplies at a moment of already-elevated food prices, while Kyiv's new proposals signal an attempt to restart diplomacy that has been largely frozen since the Iran war began.

sections.heading: North Korea Fires Ballistic Missile Ahead of US-South Korea Drills
sections.body:
North Korea launched a ballistic missile towards the Sea of Japan on Wednesday, its second weapons test in less than a week, according to Seoul and Tokyo. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missile, fired from the Wonsan area, flew more than 700km (435 miles). The launch came as South Korea and the United States announced plans to hold their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military drills starting August 17, with 18,000 South Korean soldiers taking part.

'North Korea has never simply let a South Korea-US joint military exercise pass without a response,' Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University, told AFP, calling the launch a signal that Pyongyang is closely watching the drills and could stage further provocations.
sections.whyItMatters: The test keeps the Korean Peninsula on a familiar escalation cycle just as Washington's attention and military resources are heavily committed to the Iran war, a distraction Pyongyang appears ready to exploit.

bottomLine: The day's defining development is Iraq locking in a September 30 end to the US-led coalition's military mission, a concrete step that reshapes Washington's regional footprint even as the Iran war grinds on with Hormuz traffic at a fraction of pre-war levels and the first Houthi shipping deaths of the conflict. Ukraine's strike on Russia's grain export hub and its new peace proposals to Washington, alongside North Korea's missile test, show multiple fronts moving at once. The common thread: the US is managing a widening set of commitments with a shrinking margin for error, and the gap between official claims of control and on-the-ground reality is growing harder to ignore.
